newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: New Philippine mining rules to protect environment.
newsitem.headline: New Philippine mining rules to protect environment.

text.p: The Philippines issued new rules for mining firms on Thursday to strengthen environmental laws and protect tribal land-owners as the sector prepares for a huge rush of foreign investment.

"The revisions in the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of the Philippine Mining Act are designed to strengthen our mining laws in pursuance of our thrust of environmental protection," the Department of Environment and Natural Resources said in a statement.

The new rules would seek to assuage the fears of environmentalists and indigeneous tribes of the risks in allowing mining companies from Australia, Canada, United States and Germany to explore new areas in the country, said Environment Secretary Victor Ramos.

Foreign firms have proposed investing an initial $3 billion in new Philippine mining projects, said Deogracias Contreras, executive vice president of the Chamber of Mines of the Philippines. At least 100 foreign companies have pending applications for foreign and technical assistance agreeements (FTAAs) in the country, Ramos said. Only two firms have been granted FTAAs since the Philippine Mining Act was approved in 1995.
The law promises 100 percent ownership to foreign firms in local mining projects.
Under the new rules, mining firms would be required to obtain permission from affected indigeneous peoples before exploring their ancestral lands and to give them one percent of output as royalty.

The firms are also required to contribute at least one percent of their mining and milling costs every year to community development projects and to set up post-operational land management plans for pits, waste dams, and tailings structures.
Industry officials welcomed the revisions, saying the sector can now move forward after the "lessons learned from the Marcopper accident."
The changes in the IRR have come about in the wake of the Marcopper Mining Corp accident in March in the central Philippines.

The government has said the IRR of the Philippine Mining Act, which was signed into law by President Fidel Ramos in June 1995, needed to be reviewed after tonnes of mine waste from the Marcopper mine leaked into a nearby river.

Three officials of Marcopper, a unit of Canada's Placer Dome have been charged with violations of the Philippine Mining Act, Water Code, Pollution Control Law as well as reckless imprudence resulting to damage to property because of the incident. Marcopper said the leak was an accident.
Foreign firms said the new IRR was a "leap forward" for Philippine mining.

"But we also want the government to spell out the fiscal regime that they will be adopting under the FTAA," said Malcolm Norris, chairman of the International Mining and Exploration Committee (IMEC). IMEC groups foreign investors which are interested in investing in the local mining industry.
This should include the profit sharing formula between the government and private firms and what taxes will be imposed, Norris said.
"1996 was not a good year because we did not have any rules to go by. We hope 1997 will be better with the final revisions in the IRR," Norris said.
